source.title: Minimum Operations to Sort a Permutation

teaching.hint: How many distinct arrangements can whole-array reversal and rotation actually reach from sorted order?

solution_outline.decisive_insight: Reversal changes orientation and rotation changes offset, so every reachable arrangement is a rotation of sorted or reverse-sorted order.
solution_outline.approach: Check whether the input or its reversal is a rotation of increasing order. If the input is such a rotation and zero is at index k, its cost is min(k,n-k+2). If the reversal is such a rotation and zero is at index j there, its cost is 1+min(j,n-j). Take the best applicable case, or -1 if neither applies.
solution_outline.state_and_invariant: The state of any operation sequence reduces to a cyclic offset and an orientation bit; two reversals cancel and conjugate a left rotation into a right rotation.
solution_outline.correctness: Every operation sequence has one of the two checked orientations. The allowed candidate sequences realize each possible offset with the fewest reversals and rotations, so their minimum is globally optimal.
solution_outline.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space if a reversed copy is used; an index-view implementation uses O(1) extra space.
solution_outline.pitfall: A right rotation is not directly allowed and may need two reversals around left rotations.

source_fidelity_notes: The two whole-array operations and impossibility output are explicit; no source diagram is needed.
